nameStory: The Jelly Spot Fungus gets its name from its distinctive appearance - small, translucent orange blobs that look exactly like tiny drops of amber jelly stuck to dead wood. When you first spot these glistening droplets, you might think someone spilled marmalade in the forest! The scientific name 'Dacrymyces' comes from Greek words meaning 'tear fungus,' referring to these teardrop-shaped fruiting bodies.
description: Jelly Spot Fungus is a small, gelatinous fungus that appears as bright orange to yellow, translucent blobs on dead wood. These tiny 'jelly drops' are usually only 2-8mm across - about the size of a small pea or smaller. The fungus looks almost like colorful water droplets that have been frozen in place on rotting logs and branches. Despite their small size, they often appear in groups, creating patches of orange jewels scattered across decomposing wood.

idTips.label: Jelly-like texture
idTips.description: The fruiting bodies feel exactly like firm jelly or gelatin when gently poked - they're rubbery and will bounce back when pressed, unlike harder fungi or actual tree sap

idTips.label: Bright orange color
idTips.description: Fresh specimens are brilliant orange to golden-yellow, looking almost like tiny orange gumdrops; older ones may fade to pale yellow or become more translucent

idTips.label: Small droplet shape
idTips.description: Individual blobs are tiny - typically 2-8mm across - and shaped like flattened teardrops or cushions pressed against the wood surface

idTips.label: Growing on dead wood
idTips.description: Always found on decomposing logs, branches, or stumps; never on living trees or on the ground; prefers softwood like pine and spruce

idTips.label: Clustered growth
idTips.description: Usually appears in scattered groups or lines along the wood grain, creating patches of multiple orange spots rather than single isolated blobs

idTips.label: Translucent appearance
idTips.description: The 'jellies' are semi-transparent, allowing you to see light through them; they have an almost glass-like quality when backlit

habitat: Jelly Spot Fungus thrives on dead coniferous wood throughout New England's forests, particularly favoring fallen pine, spruce, and fir logs and branches. You'll most commonly find it in moist, shaded areas of mixed or coniferous forests where decomposing wood stays damp. It's especially abundant in areas with good air circulation but protection from direct sunlight, such as forest understories and along woodland edges.

seasonality.spring: Fresh, vibrant orange fruiting bodies begin appearing on logs as moisture levels rise and temperatures warm. This is often the best time to see the most colorful specimens.
seasonality.summer: Continues producing new fruiting bodies throughout humid summer months, though specimens may dry out and shrivel during hot, dry spells, becoming less noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for observation as cool, moist conditions return. Autumn rains refresh dried specimens and stimulate new growth on recently fallen branches.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies may persist through mild winters but often freeze and thaw repeatedly, becoming less gelatinous and more difficult to identify until spring.

funFact: When Jelly Spot Fungus dries out completely during hot weather, it shrinks into tiny, hard, dark orange chips that look completely dead - but add a few drops of water and watch the magic happen as they plump back up into perfect translucent jelly drops within minutes, like nature's own instant gelatin!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with tree sap or resin droplets, but sap is usually harder, stickier, and doesn't have that bouncy jelly texture when poked. Remember: if it jiggles like Jell-O and bounces back when pressed, it's the fungus; if it's hard or sticky, it's tree sap.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'jelly fungus,' this species belongs to a completely different group than the more familiar larger jelly fungi like Witch's Butter. The Dacrymycetaceae family represents an ancient lineage of fungi with unique microscopic features that distinguish them from other gelatinous fungi.
compareHints: Since this is the primary Dacrymyces species in New England, compare it with other small jelly fungi like Witch's Butter, which is much larger, more yellow, and has a brain-like folded surface rather than simple droplet shapes. Golden Jelly Fungus (Tremella mesenterica) also grows much larger and has distinctive lobed, lettuce-like folds, while Jelly Spot maintains its simple, smooth droplet form.
